Executive summary · 27 November 2026

What conveyor scans reveal about a potato

A conveyor camera records color and depth. We tested single-view shape completion, checked how a registration pin affects predictions, and compared one view with three for surface recovery, weight and volume.

Could we improve the hidden underside?

Copying bumps from the visible side

We tried reflecting details from the top to the bottom of a smooth potato model. Only 7 of 12 development potatoes had enough usable data for the comparison. Tuning the reflection helped by about 0.10 mm there. On a separate set, error rose by 0.06 mm across 28 measurable potatoes out of 36. The uncertainty included zero, so we kept the smooth shape as our baseline.

Development resultsSeparate-cohort test

Using the conveyor to set the height

A height adjustment guided by the detailed reference lowered development error by 1.76 mm. An adjustment estimated from the camera image alone lowered error by 0.26 mm across 24 measurable potatoes out of 36 in a separate test. The uncertainty included zero. An audit of 18 acquisition groups found no independent measurement of the support surface under each potato at capture.

Height diagnosticConveyor testCalibration audit

Does pin color change the predicted shape?

How much the shape moved

On fresh test potatoes, the pin edit moved the predicted surface more than the same color change on ordinary peel in 25 of 29 cases. The average extra movement was 0.49 mm, with a 95% interval of 0.31 to 0.63 mm across recording groups. The average stayed positive at 0.40 mm against the strongest peel patch. We set a minimum of six recording groups for confirmation. With five groups, this result describes what we observed in this set.

Fresh-potato results

Whether the shape got closer

Against the detailed 3D reference, six development potatoes improved, three worsened and one tied. Average error fell by 0.13 mm. On 3R5-2 the shape moved 2.02 mm and error fell 0.43 mm. On R8-2 it moved 1.84 mm and error rose 0.22 mm.

Accuracy results
How we checked the comparison

We ran the released CoRe++ model on CPU and verified that the pin was visible to it. We applied identical color changes at the pin and at three peel patches, with depth held fixed. We matched the model's random settings across conditions over 16 repeats. Expanding the reconstruction grid removed 321 boundary contacts in 800 predictions, and the pin effect remained positive on the same 9 of 10 development potatoes.

CPU and input checksGrid-boundary check

Does the response follow the color?

We exchanged only the color pixels between the pin and a peel patch, then repeated the same color edit at each location. The depth readings stayed at their original positions.

Across ten development potatoes, the response shifted toward the transplanted pixels on 9 of 10. It fully switched in that direction for at least two of three tested locations on 8 of 10 potatoes.

One potato originally responded more to peel edits and switched in the opposite direction at all three locations. The exchanges left visible seams and sometimes a pin rim, so the results describe the effect of color in these edited images.

One-frame pilotTen-potato results and all crops

Does a second model respond the same way?

On the same ten development potatoes, pin recoloring moved the shape farther than the mean of three matched peel edits on 9/10 for CoRe++ and 3/10 for TripoSR. Both models favored the pin on 3/10, dropping to 2/10 against each model’s strongest peel patch.

Ten-potato cross-model comparison

What do three views add?

We compared the center view with three spaced RGB-D frames registered with RAFT. The same coached peel click initialized SAM 2 in both conditions.

More reference surface on ten potatoes

Coverage within 2 mm rose from 36.63% to 41.14%, a gain of 4.50 percentage points (paired 95% interval +3.71 to +5.33). The share of fused voxel centroids farther than 2 mm rose by 1.54 percentage points.

Uncertain weight and volume gains on 30 other potatoes

Fusion changed weight mean absolute error (MAE) by −0.51 g (95% interval −1.52 to +0.37) and water-displacement volume MAE by −0.14 mL (−1.10 to +0.71). The extra processing took 17.1 seconds per potato on average.

Keep the added surface and flag uncertain points. Removing all 12,144 raw outer-view points that lacked a usable comparison lowered the far-centroid rate to 4.82%, versus 5.82% after count-matched random deletion. It also lost 27.46% of the surface originally recovered beyond center (165.20 mm² per potato), versus 0.37% (2.06 mm²) after random deletion.

An intermediate frame supplied usable depth for 7,816/12,144 raw points (64.36%). These frames helped estimate pose. The independent structure-from-motion (SfM) geometry supplied the accuracy labels. Contradictions were more error-prone than agreements on 6/9 potatoes with both categories.

End-to-end fusionRemoval comparisonIntermediate-depth verification

Where should the operator click?

Click on the peel, away from the pin

On 40 development potatoes, the first human session produced 1/40 correct center masks. With an instruction to avoid the pin and the edge, the coached repeat on the same potatoes reached 40/40.

Test with a first-time operator

One new operator using the coached instruction and an annotation-derived target arrow got 45/45 correct held-out center masks (exact 95% interval 92.1% to 100%). Weight MAE was 12.26 g with SAM 2 and 12.36 g with provided masks. The weight difference interval included zero.

Prompt development and held-out tracking

Which center-frame estimate worked best?

Five estimators used the same 40 development potatoes, provided masks and fixed camera calibration. This benchmark used no measured tuber thickness. Lower mean absolute error is better.

EstimatorWeight MAE (g)Volume MAE (mL)
L0 · Silhouette16.0216.99
L1 · Frozen monocular height23.7122.75
L2 · Learned RGB height15.9216.73
L3 · Silhouette + camera-estimated height14.1815.12
L4 · RGB-D point cloud + the L3 height35.4635.92

Use the center frame for weight and volume in the tested workflow. With provided masks, L3 had the lowest errors. Use three-view fusion when the added surface matters. The SAM 2 and fusion experiments used a separate depth filter that relied on measured tuber thickness.

L0–L4 protocol and paired comparisonsIndependent acquisition audit

What is still open?

We still need to find out whether CoRe++ recognizes the pin itself and whether physically removing it changes reconstruction accuracy. The earlier underside height experiment still lacks an independent measurement of where the conveyor supported each potato. The L3 development result also needs an independent acquisition, and one operator’s SAM 2 result leaves between-operator reliability open.

Based on archived experiments. Development, fresh pin-color and held-out tracking cohorts are identified by study.
